Dear Ledgerly Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the UX Researcher II role on the AI Assistant team. I've spent over four years as a product data analyst at Cadence, a consumer fitness app, and for the past year I've been moving toward user research. You asked for product analytics experience with real exposure to user research, and that describes my background.

My most relevant work is on AI Coach, a feature that changes users' workout plans based on their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. I owned the analysis of its four-week launch test with about 180,000 users. Weekly workouts rose 8.0% (95% CI 6.1–9.9%) and 7-day retention rose 2.1 points. I also checked for a novelty effect week by week and found that the lift held through week four. That check matters for any AI feature, because early curiosity can look like lasting value.

The numbers were only part of the story. When I coded about 1,200 open-ended responses from the post-launch survey, one group of comments didn't fit the positive/neutral/negative scheme: users who "didn't understand why the plan changed." I flagged it and asked that it be reported separately from the sentiment score. Those comments are why your role interests me. When an AI system acts on personal data, satisfaction and trust are different things, and a headline metric can hide the gap between them. Workouts are lower-stakes than money, and I'd like to help Ledgerly measure that gap well.

I've been building my qualitative skills on purpose. I took notes for four user interviews our UX research team ran on AI Coach and set up a synthesis format that kept timestamped quotes separate from interpretation. My HCI degree included a semi-structured interview study and a usability test with eight participants. I haven't led a full qualitative study in industry yet, and I want to grow into that work in this role. What I bring now is strong experiment analysis, SQL, survey coding, and experience turning findings into readouts that product teams act on.

I'd welcome the chance to talk about how I could help Ledgerly understand and measure trust in its AI Assistant.

Best,
Riley Nakamura

**Statement of Purpose — Riley Nakamura**
**PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences — Fall 2027**

In the summer of 2025, I was coding about 1,200 open-ended survey responses about AI Coach, a feature at the fitness app Cadence that changes users' workout plans based on their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. The product manager wanted one sentiment number for the launch deck, and the final figure was 72% positive. One group of responses didn't fit any of my sentiment codes. Those users weren't happy or unhappy with the feature. They *didn't understand why their plan had changed.*

That group ended up in the appendix. I've kept thinking about it, because it pointed to something the rest of my analysis had missed. I had owned the analysis of AI Coach's launch experiment: four weeks, about 180,000 users. Treatment users completed 8.0% more weekly workouts (95% CI 6.1–9.9%), and 7-day retention rose 2.1 percentage points. I checked for a novelty effect, and the lift held through week four. By every metric we tracked, the feature worked. Yet some of the people using it couldn't explain what it was doing to them, and nothing we measured would have caught that.

I want to pursue a PhD to study that gap. My research question is how people understand, and decide whether to trust, AI systems that act on their personal data. I'm also interested in how we should measure that understanding, since engagement metrics can stay high while it's missing.

**Research interests**

I'm drawn to three related questions:

1. **Making sense of adaptive systems.** AI Coach didn't just recommend. It changed users' plans without being asked. When a system adapts on its own, how do people notice the changes, explain them to themselves, and decide whether to go along? How do those explanations change over weeks of use?

2. **Sensitive personal data.** Sleep and heart-rate data feel more personal than clicks. Does the type of data a system uses change how much explanation people expect, or how they react when an inference seems wrong?

3. **Measuring trust and understanding.** In industry, AI features are judged mostly on behavior: retention, engagement, conversion. I want to develop measures that capture whether people understand and appropriately trust these systems, and to test how those measures relate to the behavioral metrics teams already use.

I expect to use mixed methods: interviews and diary studies to see how people's understanding forms over time, plus surveys and field experiments to test what we learn at scale.

**Preparation**

I should be direct about where I'm starting from. I don't have research publications, and my formal research experience comes from my undergraduate HCI coursework at Riverside State University. In User Research Methods, I ran semi-structured interviews with six students about how they used campus apps and synthesized the findings into an affinity diagram and report. For my capstone, my four-person team redesigned the campus library app and ran a usability test with eight students.

My stronger preparation comes from four years as a product data analyst at Cadence. I've owned the analysis for about 20 A/B tests a year: writing analysis plans, running power calculations, and presenting results to product teams. That work taught me to care about study design. Once a PM wanted to run a one-week test on a paywall change. My power calculation showed it needed about four weeks to detect the effect we cared about, so I proposed a three-week test with a pre-registered primary metric, and the PM agreed. I also write SQL and Python (pandas, statsmodels) every day for cohort analysis and modeling.

In 2025 I volunteered to take notes for four interviews our UX research team ran on AI Coach. The researcher led the interviews and the synthesis. My job was capturing what participants said, and I set up a notes format that kept timestamped quotes separate from my interpretations. That month confirmed for me that I wanted to do this kind of work, and I want the training to lead it myself.

**Goals**

After the PhD, I hope to do research, in academia or an industry research lab, that changes how AI features in health, finance, and other personal domains are evaluated. My goal is for "do people understand what this system is doing to them?" to become a standard question alongside "did it move the metric?" I first noticed that gap as an analyst, and I'd like to spend the next five years learning to study it properly.

**Statement of Purpose — Riley Nakamura**
**PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences — Fall 2027**

In 2025 I sat in on four user interviews about AI Coach, a feature in the fitness app where I work as a data analyst. AI Coach changes people's workout plans based on their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. I was there to take notes. Mostly I was listening to people try to explain, in their own words, what the app was doing for them. It was more interesting than any dashboard I've built.

Around the same time, I was coding about 1,200 open-ended responses from our post-launch survey. Roughly one in ten said something like "it changed my plan and I have no idea why," or asked how the app knew they'd slept badly. A couple of people said they'd turned off health-data sharing. In the launch deck, all of it became one number: 72% positive.

The metric and what people were saying felt like two different products. That still bugs me. It's the main reason I'm applying.

**What I want to study**

I want to understand what people think is happening when an app uses their own data to make choices for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say.

Some questions I keep coming back to:

- When a system changes something without asking, how do people notice? How do they explain it to themselves?
- When does an inference feel helpful, and when does it feel intrusive? Easing someone's workout after a bad night is reasonable. It's also a little unsettling that the app knows.
- When people turn off data sharing, what are they reacting to? The data, the decision, or not being asked?
- What does having a say actually look like? Explanations, controls, the ability to undo, or something else?

I'm not interested in making these systems more engaging or their recommendations more accurate. Plenty of people work on that. I'm interested in the people on the other end.

I expect this work to start with interviews and diary studies, following people over weeks as their understanding forms. Then I'd test what we learn at a larger scale. My questions aren't fully formed yet. Learning how to sharpen them is part of why I want a PhD.

**Where I'm starting from**

I don't have publications. My research experience comes from undergraduate coursework in Riverside State's HCI track: an interview study with six students about campus apps, and a capstone usability test with eight. They were small projects.

Since 2022 I've been a product analyst at Cadence. The job taught me two things. A well-designed experiment can tell you a lot. A clean result can also leave out most of what users actually experienced. I want to do research that takes both seriously.

**Why a PhD**

A research job would mostly have me answering whatever the product team needs that quarter. The questions above don't fit in a quarter, and they aren't always the ones a product team wants answered. I want the time and training to study them properly.

**Why Khoury**
